misconceptions.believed: That the boss fight was playable. S019, S020 and S021 all shipped against it and each verified the loop end to end; S020 drove it through a real pty and watched BOSS DOWN.
misconceptions.revealed_by: Running 'boss w1-boss-pipeline --live' with no arguments, for the first time, in order to write a tutorial about it. It stops dead on step one and offers nothing.
misconceptions.corrected_to: Every one of those verifications used --solution broken.py, a file I wrote whose bug was a KeyError. A crash is the dramatic failure, not the common one. The starter, which is what every player begins with, fails by returning the wrong value, and that path had no repair, no explanation and no way forward. The same blind spot hid a second bug: I never cleared step one from the starter, so I never saw that step two arrives with no stub.
misconceptions.generalisable_lesson: M1's shape a third time. M1 was scoring a system with a good solution and never a bad one; M35 was checking that a step did not crash and never that it answered; this is verifying a game with a fixture and never with its own front door. Use the thing the way its user will, not the way your test harness does. S020's journal listed 'Anyone but me has played a boss fight - nobody has - UNVERIFIED' in my own words; flagging a risk is not retiring it, and an UNVERIFIED re-copied forward is a decision to keep not looking.

decisions.decision: A step that answers wrongly offers a repair and re-runs from the top
decisions.rationale: The common failure has to be the repairable one, and there is nothing to resume once the run has completed. Both paths spend from the same pool through one function.

decisions.decision: Each step's stub is appended to the player's buffer when they reach it
alternatives: Hand out the whole skeleton up front
decisions.rationale: A boss is one growing file. The whole skeleton gives away the shape of steps they have not reached; no stub asks them to guess a signature the game never showed.

decisions.decision: A wrong answer opens the pane on the function, with 'expected ... got ...'
decisions.rationale: There is no offending line, and a percentage cannot be acted on. Ordinary levels already show expected versus got, so this is consistency rather than a new disclosure.

decisions.decision: A scripted --fix is spent per attempt; a typed repair is not
decisions.rationale: A file cannot change its mind, so re-reading it loops. A person can, and is sitting right there.

decisions.decision: docs/PLAYING.md is written as a playtest guide, not a tutorial
decisions.rationale: The mechanics are tested and the feel is not. A tutorial that hides which numbers are guesses invites the reader to treat all of them as settled.

friction.description: Driving the repair pane from a pty needed bracketed paste rather than typed characters, because the buffer auto-indents and re-indenting pasted Python fights it. Correct behaviour for a person and for a paste; it only looks like friction from a test harness.
Holding ctrl-k is the only way to clear a function before rewriting it. It works and the tutorial documents it, but 'hold a key thirty times' is not a design. Q78.

handoff.state: The boss fight is playable from the starter with nothing but the game, verified by playing the whole thing through a pty and typing every line. Two blocking bugs fixed: a wrong answer was unrepairable, and the buffer never grew so step two arrived with no stub. docs/PLAYING.md walks a player through it. 985 tests green unpinned, 961 pinned, verify clean on 45 reference runs.
handoff.next_action: The user plays it. Nothing here is worth building on until someone who is not me has had a fight. Q79 is the first thing they will hit and it needs their answer rather than a patch: every starter answers wrongly, so every step costs a repair and BOSS DOWN is unreachable on a first play, while W6's waypoint text ties HP to first-try completions. After that, T3 W7, boss scoring at 40/30/30, still the only waypoint between T3 and its exit criteria.

open_questions.question: Two events land on one line when it raises. Should the display merge them?
Timeline holds Step objects for a live run and dicts for a recorded one.
An edit past step 400 fast-forwards against a truncated original.
Divergence rate over real play is measurable and uncollected.
The pane shows locals but not the expected value, except now it does for a wrong answer (D151). Should the crash path show it too, or is that handing over the answer?
Which of the remaining non-negotiables can be given a test?
The heal curve and pool size were chosen by argument, not playtest.
W8 is a waypoint no exit criterion points at. Does T3 land without it?
Clearing a function before rewriting it means holding ctrl-k. Should the pane have a 'replace this function' affordance, or is a real editor's worth of editing out of scope for a fight?

Every starter answers wrongly, so every step costs a repair and BOSS DOWN is unreachable on a first play. W6's waypoint text ties HP to first-try completions and normal play has none. Is a starter meant to be a failing stub here, or should a boss step start from something that runs?
